title: Anticipatory grief after the death: grieving before and still being undone after

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source afterward/bereavement/funeral-language synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no individual legal, financial, funeral, clinical, mental-health, or ritual advice.
limitations: Public sources support broad vocabulary and practical context only; they do not supply consented room texture.
This record must not become legal, estate, financial, funeral, clinical, mental-health, diagnosis, ritual, or crisis advice.
Local law, institutional policy, funeral-home/cemetery/crematory requirements, clinicians, mental-health professionals, guardians, tradition holders, and the person’s wishes govern actual decisions.

moment.plain_scene: A caregiver may have been grieving for months or years before the death, yet still be shocked, numb, relieved, devastated, guilty, or newly destabilized after the person dies.
ordinary_language_queries: I grieved before death but still feel destroyed
why am I shocked when death was expected

content_layers.observation_text: A caregiver may have been grieving for months or years before the death, yet still be shocked, numb, relieved, devastated, guilty, or newly destabilized after the person dies.
content_layers.source_synthesis: HFA notes grief can begin before death when losses mount; CDC supports complex emotions and bodily changes in grief. This record separates pre-loss grief from the false idea that expected death should make grief simple.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: The archive must resist the phrase “at least you had time.” Time before death can be a gift, burden, exhaustion, rehearsal, or none of these.

what_this_is_not: not a claim that expected death is easier
not a rule about relief, guilt, shock, or acceptance
uncertainties: Caregiver burden, dementia, long illness, estrangement, dependence, finances, and cultural duty all change anticipatory grief.
Relief can be loving, shame-filled, practical, or complicated.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should make the phrase findable, orient the reader to why the moment is common enough to name, and then stop before giving personal legal, financial, funeral, mental-health, clinical, or ritual advice.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner or researcher surface should collect who had authority, what words were used, what the setting required, what the family understood, where conflict or exclusion appeared, and which local/professional supports were involved.
language_notes: Do not treat grief as a stage, task, timetable, performance, or disorder unless a qualified diagnostic context exists.
Keep legal, funeral, financial, child, and ritual content jurisdiction- and authority-bound.
Preserve ordinary words the bereaved use, including euphemism, anger, numbness, absence, and administrative speech.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the afterward, funeral/disposition, administrative-burden, and grief-language layer. It requires domain review before any public surface uses it.
